# The Anharmonic Origin of the Giant Thermal Expansion of NaBr

Y. Shen,1, ∗C. N. Saunders,1 C. M. Bernal,1 D. L. Abernathy,2 M. E. Manley,3 and B. Fultz1, †

1Department of Applied Physics and Materials Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA 2Neutron Scattering Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee 37831, USA 3Materials Science and Technology Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee 37831, USA (Dated: September 10, 2019)

All phonons in a single crystal of NaBr were measured by inelastic neutron scattering at temperatures of 10, 300 and 700 K. Even at 300 K the phonons, especially the longitudinal-optical (LO) phonons, showed large shifts in frequencies, and showed large broadenings in energy owing to anharmonicity. Ab initio computations were ﬁrst performed with the quasiharmonic approximation (QHA), in which the phonon frequencies depend only on V , and on T only insofar as it alters V by thermal expansion. This QHA was an unqualiﬁed failure for predicting the temperature dependence of phonon frequencies, even 300 K, and the thermal expansion was in error by a factor of four. Ab initio computations that included both anharmonicity and quasiharmonicity successfully predicted both the temperature dependence of phonons and the large thermal expansion of NaBr. The frequencies of LO phonon modes decrease signiﬁcantly with temperature owing to the real part of the phonon self-energy from explicit anhamonicity, originating from the cubic anharmonicity of nearest-neighbor Na-Br bonds. Anharmonicity is not a correction to the QHA predictions of thermal expansion and thermal phonon shifts, but dominates the behavior.

Thermal expansion, a fundamental thermophysical property, originates primarily from a competition between the elastic energy of expansion and the phonon entropy, which usually increases beyond harmonic behavior as a solid expands. Thermal expansion can be calculated readily in the quasiharmonic approximation (QHA), which assumes that phonon frequencies depend only on volume [1–6]. The QHA theory of thermal expansion is textbook content and is logically self-consistent. It ignores explicit anharmonicity, where phonon frequencies also change with temperature at a ﬁxed volume [7, 8]. Some calculations include anharmonicity as a small correction to the QHA, but the relative importance of anharmonicity is not yet settled [2, 9]. We recently found that the QHA gave the wrong sign for the temperature dependence of most phonons in silicon [10]. This shows that the QHA is physically incomplete, even though it did predict correctly the thermal expansion. Here we report a more compelling inelastic neutron scattering (INS) experiment to test predictions of phonons and thermal expansion in a diﬀerent material, sodium bromide (NaBr). Like other alkali halides with the rocksalt structure [11–13], NaBr has received special attention owing to its cubic structure and highly ionic bonding. The INS data from a single crystal of NaBr were acquired with the time-of-ﬂight spectrometer, ARCS [14], at the Spallation Neutron Source at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, using neutrons with an incident energy of 30 meV. Data were collected from 201 rotations of the crystal in increments of 0.5◦about the vertical [001] axis. Data reduction gave the 4D scattering func-

FIG. 2. Thermal expansion of NaBr. The ab initio QHA (blue solid line) and anharmonic calculations (red solid circles) are compared with experimental results [28–31]. There is a large discrepancy between the measurements and the QHA predictions, while results from the sTDEP method are in close agreement with the experiments.

Some calculated phonon spectral weights are compared to experimental measurements in Fig. 1 along directions of high symmetry. At 10 K, all calculations agree with each other and with the experimental measurements. At higher temperatures, the acoustic dispersions below 14 meV show some softening, especially at 700 K, but are not broadened so much as the optical modes. The optical modes show large broadening at 300 K, and major changes in shape at 700 K. The temperature dependence of the optical dispersions is largely captured by the spectral weight calculated by sTDEP, but only a minor part of the softening is predicted by the QHA calculations (and none of the broadening owing to its assumption of noninteracting modes). The quadratic term from sTDEP (with Φαβ ij in Eq. 2) was used to calculate the dispersions shown as black dashed lines in Fig. 1a-c. By itself, this term does not reproduce the thermal phonon softening. The largest contribution to the temperature shift of the spectral weight is from the real part of the cubic term, obtained as a Kramers–Kronig transformation of the imaginary part of the self-energy as explained in the Supplemental Material [17] with Eq. 51. The imaginary part of the phonon self-energy from this cubic term is responsible for the surprisingly-large energy broadening of the longitudinal optical (LO) phonons at 300 K and especially at 700 K. The experimental inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements (see Fig. 1) were ﬁtted to give the energy shifts of LO phonons presented in Table I. The QHA accounts for only a small part of the experimental shifts, but the anharmonic calculations are much more successful. The spectral intensities at the L-point are shown in Fig. 3a. All phonons at the L-point soften and broaden signiﬁcantly with temperature. Spectra from the longi-

tudinal acoustic (LA) and transverse optic (TO) phonon modes merge into one broad peak at 700 K. The longitudinal optical (LO) peak broadens signiﬁcantly, but its large thermal softening is still evident. Figure 3b shows that the real part of the self-energy of the LO phonon at the L-point is approximately –3.5 meV at 700 K, so phonon-phonon anharmonicity dominates the thermal shift of this mode (the LO mode has a phonon energy of 19 meV at the L-point from sTDEP). The Supplemental Material [17] shows some of the spectral weights in more detail. There are diﬀerences between experiment and the sTDEP calculations at 700 K, especially halfway between Γ and L between 16 and 23 meV. Some anharmonic effects in NaBr are too large to be predicted accurately by the sTDEP method. To understand the origin of the anharmonicity at 700 K, the cubic irreducible force constants (IFCs) for the three-body interactions within the ﬁrst ten coordination shells were individually set to zero while recalculating phonon lineshapes at diﬀerent Q. Figure 3c shows how two related IFCs dominate the lineshapes. They correspond to the nearest-neighbor cubic interactions of degenerate triplets (NaNaBr and/or NaBrBr) in the [100] direction (i.e. along the Na-Br bond direction). (By translational invariance, Φααα NaNaBr = −Φααα NaBrBr.) When these force constants are switched oﬀ, the phonon lineshapes revert to narrow Lorentzian functions typical of weakly anharmonic solids, and these Lorentzian peaks are at energies similar to those from the QHA calculations. The dominance of Φααα NaNaBr = −Φααα NaBrBr on the phonon anharmonicity was found for phonons at all other points in reciprocal space, as shown in the Supplemental Material [17]. The physics of thermal expansion requires volume and temperature derivatives of F(V, T), speciﬁcally ∂2F/ (∂V ∂T) = −β BT . ## B. Phonon Statistical Mechanics

We address the underlying physics by calculating the phonon free energy, ignoring possible contributions from electronic or magnetic excitations. The key quantities are the energies {ℏωi}, where ωi is the frequency of a phonon added to the ith vibrational mode. In general, this frequency depends on V and T, ωi(V, T). In the “quasiharmonic approximation” (QHA), the ωi and the phonon free energy depend only on V . In the QHA, the eﬀects of temperature are only from the occupancies of phonon modes. The QHA is convenient for calculating thermal expansion, requiring only a set of mode Gr¨uneisen parameters. It was recently proved that the QHA gives the leading term of the quantity ∂F/∂V [1], also [2]. This does not guarantee that the QHA gives the leading term of the thermal expansion coeﬃcient, however, because a temperature derivative is still needed. (For example, consider the functional y = y0 + ∆y, where y0 = 100 + 0.001 sin x and ∆y = sin x. Here the x-derivative is dominated by the small term ∆y, rather than the leading term y0.) Less well known are anharmonic theories of thermal expansion developed with many-body theory [3, 4]. To our knowledge, there has been no direct comparison of thermal expansion from the QHA and anharmonic theory, so the goal of this section is an comparison of the relative importance of each. Ignoring the entropy from free electrons or magnetic excitations, for a simple solid with N atoms the Helmholtz free energy originates with the electronic energy, i.e., the internal energy of the lattice, U0, plus the free energy from phonons

## II. INELASTIC NEUTRON SCATTERING EXPERIMENTS

The INS measurements used a high-purity single crystal of NaBr. Crystal quality was checked by X-ray and neutron diﬀraction. The INS data were acquired with the time-of-ﬂight Wide Angular-Range Chopper Spectrometer, ARCS, at the Spallation Neutron Source at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The neutrons had an incident energy of 30 meV. The single crystal of [001] orientation was suspended in an aluminum holder, which was mounted in a closedcycle helium refrigerator for the 10 K measurement, and a low-background electrical resistance vacuum furnace for measurements at 300 and 700 K. For each measurement, time-of-ﬂight neutron data was collected from 201 rotations of the crystal in increments of 0.5◦about the vertical axis. Data reduction gave the 4D scattering function S(Q, ε), where Q is the 3D wave-vector and ε is the phonon energy (from the neutron energy loss). Measurements with an empty can were performed to evaluate the background. To correct for nonlinearities of the ARCS instrument, oﬀsets of the q-grid were corrected to ﬁrst order by ﬁtting a set of 45 in situ Bragg diﬀractions, which were transformed to their theoretical positions in the reciprocal space of the NaBr structure. The linear transformation matrix had only a small deviation (less than 0.02) from the identity matrix, showing that the original data had good quality and the linear correction for q-oﬀsets was adequate. After subtracting the empty-can background and removing multiphonon scattering calculated with the incoherent approximation (discussed below), the intensities from the higher Brillouin zones were folded back into an irreducible wedge in the ﬁrst Brillouin zone to obtain the spectral intensities shown in Fig. 2 in the main text. ## IV. PHONONS AWAY FROM HIGH SYMMETRY LINES

# Density of $\mu$ -ordinary Primes for K3 Surfaces

**Authors:** Trung Can1, Yuxin Lin2 Email address: ctttrung@hcmus.edu.vn Email address: bennylin@umich.edu Address: [1] University of Science, Vietnam National University, Ho Chi Minh City Address: [2] University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

## Abstract

By a result of Bogomolov and Zarhin, a K3 surface $X$ over a number field $L$ has ordinary reduction at a density 1 set of primes after passing to a finite extension of $L$ . In this paper, we refine this result for non-CM K3 surfaces whose transcendental Hodge structure has endomorphism field $F$ abelian over $\mathbb{Q}$ . We further assume a condition on the connected components of the $l$ -adic monodromy group of $X$ , and, when $F$ is totally real, a parity condition on the rank of the transcendental lattice over $F$ . Under these assumptions, we prove that the set of primes of $L$ at which $X$ has $\mu$ -ordinary reduction has density $1$ . As a corollary, the set of primes of $L$ at which $X$ has ordinary reduction has density $1/[FL:L]$ . We include explicit examples of K3 surfaces satisfying these conditions.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Density of ordinary primes

Let $A$ be an abelian variety over a number field $L$ . For all but finitely many primes $\mathfrak{p}$ of $L$ , the variety $A$ has good reduction at $\mathfrak{p}$ . The reduction $A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is called ordinary if its Newton polygon has only the slopes $0$ and $1$ . A conjecture generally attributed to Serre asserts that, after passing to a suitable finite extension of $L$ , the set of primes at which $A$ has ordinary reduction has density $1$ .11 1 Throughout, density means natural density. The conjecture is known for elliptic curves (Serre [14]) and for abelian surfaces (Ogus [10]), but it remains open in general.

The same question can be asked for other classes of varieties. Let $X$ be a K3 surface over $L$ and let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime of good reduction. The reduction $X_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is ordinary if its Newton polygon has slopes $0,1,2$ . Bogomolov and Zarhin [2] proved the analog of Serre’s conjecture for K3 surfaces: after a finite extension of $L$ , the surface $X$ has ordinary reduction at a set of primes of density $1$ .

Neither statement says which extension is needed or what the density of ordinary primes is over $L$ itself. For an elliptic curve $E$ , the density is $1$ if all endomorphisms of $E_{\overline{L}}$ are defined over $L$ , and $1/2$ otherwise. Sawin [13] expressed the density of ordinary primes of an abelian surface over $L$ in terms of the component group of its $l$ -adic monodromy group and showed that it always equals $1$ , $1/2$ , or $1/4$ . Cantoral-Farfán et al [3] considered absolutely simple abelian varieties whose geometric endomorphism algebra is a CM field $F$ acting with simple signature. When $F/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois, they compute the density of ordinary primes over $L$ explicitly. When $F/\mathbb{Q}$ is abelian, they show that the reduction is $\mu$ -ordinary at a density 1 set of primes of $L$ . In this paper, we prove results of the same kind for K3 surfaces.

### 1.2. $\mu$ -ordinary reduction and main results

Let $X$ be a K3 surface over $L$ and fix an embedding $L\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ . Let $T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\subset H^{2}(X_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Q})$ denote the transcendental part of the cohomology, and let

$$ F:=\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{Hdg}}\bigl(T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\bigr) $$

be its algebra of Hodge endomorphisms. By a theorem of Zarhin [18], $F$ is a number field, and it is either totally real or CM.

Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime of $L$ of good reduction, with residue characteristic $p$ . The action of $F$ constrains the Newton polygon of $X_{\mathfrak{p}}$ in a way that depends on how $p$ decomposes in $F$ . The lowest Newton polygon compatible with this constraint is called the $\mu$ -ordinary Newton polygon. For K3 surfaces it is the polygon of height $d$ , with slopes $\bigl(1-\tfrac{1}{d},\,1,\,1+\tfrac{1}{d}\bigr)$ , where the integer $d$ is determined by the splitting of $p$ in $F$ (see Section 2). In particular, if $p$ splits completely in $F$ , then $d=1$ and the $\mu$ -ordinary polygon is the ordinary one.

At primes where the $\mu$ -ordinary polygon is not ordinary, ordinary reduction cannot occur, so $\mu$ -ordinary reduction is the best one can hope for. This leads to a refinement of Serre’s question: does $X$ have $\mu$ -ordinary reduction at a density 1 set of primes of $L$ , without any extension of the base field?

Let $L^{\text{conn}}$ denote the smallest extension of $L$ over which the $l$ -adic monodromy group $G_{X,l}$ of $X$ becomes connected. Our main result answers the refined question under the following assumptions.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $X$ be a K3 surface over a number field $L$ without complex multiplication, and let $F=\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{Hdg}}(T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}})$ . Assume that

- (1) $F/\mathbb{Q}$ is an abelian extension;

- (2) $L^{\text{conn}}\subseteq FL$ ;

- (3) if $F$ is totally real, then $\dim_{F}T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is even.

Then the set of primes of $L$ at which $X$ has $\mu$ -ordinary reduction has density $1$ .

The $\mu$ -ordinary and ordinary Newton polygons coincide exactly at the primes of $L$ lying over rational primes that split completely in $F$ . Hence Theorem 1.1 determines the density of ordinary primes over $L$ .

#### Corollary 1.2.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.1, the set of primes of $L$ at which $X$ has ordinary reduction has density $1/[FL:L]$ .

Corollary 1.2 refines the theorem of Bogomolov and Zarhin in this setting. It identifies $FL$ as an extension over which ordinary reduction occurs at a density 1 set of primes, and it computes the density of ordinary primes over $L$ itself.

In [3], the endomorphism field is assumed to be CM. In contrast, Theorem 1.1 also covers the case where $F$ is totally real, provided that $\dim_{F}T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is even.

For K3 surfaces, Sawin has proved in an unpublished manuscript that $\mu$ -ordinary reduction occurs at a set of primes of density $1$ . The present work was carried out independently. Our argument is accessible and self-contained; in particular, we computed the relevant trace function explicitly on the relevant orthogonal groups; we learned of Sawin’s manuscript only after our results were obtained. As described in [3, Remark 4.20], Sawin’s argument applies to arbitrary K3 surfaces over number fields and to Kuga–Satake abelian varieties.

### 1.3. Strategy of the proof

We follow the $\ell$ -adic method of Serre, Katz–Ogus, Sawin, in the form developed by Cantoral-Farfán et al [3], and adapt it to K3 surfaces. The proof has three key steps.

- (1) We construct a conjugacy-invariant algebraic function on $G_{X,l}$ that detects $\mu$ -ordinary reduction. Combined with the Weil bounds and Serre’s Chebotarev density theorem, this reduces the density question to showing that the function is non-constant on every connected component of $G_{X,l}$ .

- (2) Using the assumptions that $F/\mathbb{Q}$ is abelian and $L^{\text{conn}}\subseteq FL$ , we realize the component group of $G_{X,l}$ as a subgroup of the Weyl group of the orthogonal group.

- (3) An explicit matrix computation then shows that the function is non-constant on each connected component.

### 1.4. Organization of the paper

Section 2 collects background and notation on $\mu$ -ordinary Newton polygons, $l$ -adic monodromy groups and Mumford–Tate groups of K3 surfaces. In Section 3 we construct the invariant that detects $\mu$ -ordinary reduction and establish its properties. Section 4 contains the proof of Theorem 1.1. Finally, in Example 4.5 we construct explicit families of K3 surfaces to which Theorem 1.1 applies.

## 2. Preliminaries

### 2.1. K3 Hodge structure and orthogonal Shimura datum

Let $X$ be a K3 surface over a number field $L$ . Let $\overline{L}$ denote an algebraic closure of $L$ . Fix an embedding $L\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ . The cohomology group $H^{2}(X_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{\mathbb{Z}})$ is of rank $22$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ with symmetric bilinear form $\Psi$ induced by Poincaré duality. Let $\text{NS}(X_{\mathbb{C}})$ be the Néron–Severi group of $X_{\mathbb{C}}$ and define the transcendental part by

$$ T(X):=\text{NS}(X_{\mathbb{C}})^{\perp}\subset H^{2}(X_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Z}), $$

where the orthogonal complement is taken with respect to $\Psi$ .

Let $V:=T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ , then $\Psi$ restricts to a symmetric bilinear form on $V$ . The Hodge decomposition on $H^{2}(X_{\mathbb{C}},\mathbb{Q})$ induces a rational Hodge structure on $V$ . We define $\mathcal{E}(X)$ to be the endomorphism algebra of $T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ preserving this Hodge structure. That is,

$$ \mathcal{E}(X):=\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm{Hdg}}(T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}) $$

Let $\mathbb{S}=\operatorname{Res}_{\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{G}_{m}$ be the Deligne torus. Let $h:\mathbb{S}\to\mathrm{GL}(V_{\mathbb{R}})$ be the structure homomorphism of the rational polarized K3 Hodge structure on $(V,\Psi)$ . Since the Hodge structure is polarized by $\Psi$ , the morphism $h$ factors through the group of orthogonal similitude $\mathrm{GO}(V,\Psi)_{\mathbb{R}}$ . The triple $(V,\Psi,h)$ determines an orthogonal Shimura datum $\mathcal{D}=(\mathrm{GO}(V,\Psi),\mathcal{X})$ where $\mathcal{X}$ is the $\mathrm{GO}(V,\Psi)(\mathbb{R})$ -conjugacy class of $h$ .

#### Assumption 1.

Throughout the paper, we assume that:

- (A1) $F=\mathcal{E}(X)$ is isomorphic to an abelian field extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ ;

- (A2) $X$ does not have complex multiplication, and if $F$ is totally real, then we also assume that $\dim_{F}(T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}})$ is even.

#### Notation 2.1.

Given $X$ satisfying $(A1)$ and $(A2)$ :

- • Let $*$ denote the complex conjugation on $F$ and let $F_{0}$ be the fixed subfield of $F$ under $*$ . Notice that if $F$ is totally real, then $*$ is the identity and $F_{0}=F$ .

- • Let $m=[F_{0}:\mathbb{Q}]$ and

$$ n=\begin{cases}\dim_{F}(T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}),&\text{if $F$ is CM},\\[4.0pt] \frac{1}{2}\dim_{F}(T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}),&\text{if $F$ is totally real}.\end{cases} $$

Notice that $2mn=\text{rank}_{\mathbb{Z}}(T(X))$ .

Now let $F=\mathcal{E}(X)$ . Then $F$ acts on $V$ , and we define the $F$ -linear orthogonal similitude group by

$$ \mathrm{GO}_{F}(V,\Psi):=\operatorname{Cent}_{\mathrm{GO}(V,\Psi)}(F) $$

Equivalently, for every $\mathbb{Q}$ -algebra $R$ ,

$$ \mathrm{GO}_{F}(V,\Psi)(R)=\left\{g\in\mathrm{GL}_{F\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}R}(V\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}R)\ \middle|\ \exists c(g)\in R^{\times}\text{ such that }\Psi(gu,gv)=c(g)\Psi(u,v)\text{ for all }u,v\right\}. $$

Let $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})$ be the orthogonal Shimura variety attached to Shimura datum $\mathcal{D}$ . Under the Assumption 1, the reflex field $E$ is contained in $FL$ . Since $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})$ has a canonical model over its reflex field $E$ , it is defined over $FL$ . Hence, for every prime $\mathfrak{p}\in FL$ , we can consider the reduction of $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})$ at $\mathfrak{p}$ .

In this paper, we focus on the set of primes in $L$ with the following properties:

#### Definition 2.2 (The set $S$ ).

Given $X/L$ a K3 surface, let $S$ be the set of primes $\mathfrak{p}$ in $L$ satisfying the following:

- • $X$ has good reduction at $\mathfrak{p}$ ;

- • Let $p=\mathfrak{p}\cap\mathbb{Z}$ . Then $p$ is unramified in $F/\mathbb{Q}$

- • $\mathfrak{p}$ has degree 1.

Now, let $p$ be a rational prime that is unramified in $F$ . Since $F/\mathbb{Q}$ is abelian, we have a well-defined Frobenius element $\text{Fr}_{p}$ in $\text{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ .

#### Notation 2.3.

Given such a prime $p$ , we set:

- • Let $d$ be the order of $\text{Fr}_{p}$ in $\mathrm{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ . In particular, $d\mid[F:\mathbb{Q}]$ .

- • Let $K$ be the fixed field of $F$ under $\text{Fr}_{p}$ . That is, $K=F^{\langle\text{Fr}_{p}\rangle}$ . In particular, $K$ is the largest subfield of $F$ for which $p$ splits completely.

Notice that $d=[F:K]$ .

#### Definition 2.4 (Natural density).

For a number field $L/\mathbb{Q}$ , let $A$ , $B$ be sets of primes in $L$ . Then, we define the natural density of set $A$ in $B$ as follows:

$$ \rho(A:B)=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\#\{\mathfrak{p}\in A,N^{L}_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathfrak{p}\leq x\}}{\#\{\mathfrak{p}\in B,N^{L}_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathfrak{p}\leq x\}} $$

In particular, if $B=\{\mathfrak{p}\in\text{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{L})\}$ , then we define the density of $A$ as:

$$ \rho(A):=\rho(A:B) $$

Since primes of degree one have density $1$ , the set $S$ has density $1$ in $L$ .

For $\mathfrak{p}\in S$ , let $p=\mathfrak{p}\cap\mathbb{Z}$ . Then, $p$ is unramified in $E$ and hence is a prime of good reduction for $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})$ . Hence, we can consider the special fibre at $p$ given by $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ .

### 2.2. The $\mu$ -ordinary Newton polygon of K3 surface with additional structure

Let $X/L$ be a K3 surface satisfying $(A1)$ and $(A2)$ . Let $\mathfrak{p}\in S$ be a good prime for $X$ and let $p=\mathfrak{p}\cap\mathbb{Z}$ . Let $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ be the residue field of $\mathfrak{p}$ . By assumption on $S$ , we have that $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}=\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . Let $X_{\mathfrak{p}}$ be the reduction of $X$ mod $\mathfrak{p}$ . Let $W(\mathbb{F}_{p})\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ be the ring of Witt vectors on $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ .

Let $\varphi$ denote the Frobenius action on the crystalline cohomology group $H^{2}_{cris}(X_{\mathfrak{p}}/W(\mathbb{F}_{p}))$ . Then, the Newton polygon $\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(X)$ is the multiset of the p-adic valuations of the eigenvalues of $\varphi$ . It can equivalently be computed as the $p$ -adic valuation of the eigenvalues of Frobenius acting on $H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ for $l\neq p$ . Given a Newton polygon $\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}$ , we call $\lambda\in\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}$ a slope and the number of times $\lambda$ appears in $\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}$ its multiplicity.

When $X/L$ is a K3 surface, since $H^{2}_{cris}(X_{\mathfrak{p}}/W(\mathbb{F}_{p}))$ has rank $22$ over $W(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ , $\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(X)$ has length $22$ . Moreover, by [8], there exists an integer $h:=h(X)\in\{1,2,\dots,10\}$ such that $\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(X)$ has slopes $(1-1/h,1,1+1/h)$ with multiplicities $(h,22-2h,h)$ , or $\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(X)$ has slope $1$ with multiplicity $22$ .

Recall that we can construct an orthogonal Shimura variety $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})$ from $X$ with good reduction at $\mathfrak{p}\in S$ . In [12, Theorem 4.2], Rapoport and Richartz described the lowest Newton polygon occurring in the special fibre $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ in terms of the splitting behavior of $p$ in $F/\mathbb{Q}$ . In our case, $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})$ parametrizes K3 Hodge structures on $T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ , which has rank $2mn$ . Hence the Newton polygons occurring on the special fibre $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ record the Frobenius slopes coming from the transcendental part of $H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})$ . The Néron–Severi part has rank $22-2mn$ and contributes only slope $1$ . Therefore, for each Newton polygon occurring on $\text{Sh}(\mathcal{D})_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}$ , we adjoin $22-2mn$ copies of slope $1$ .

We define $\mu_{\mathfrak{p}}$ to be the lowest length- $22$ Newton polygon obtained in this way. Thus, $\mu_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is the lowest Newton polygon that can occur for a K3 surface with the prescribed additional $F$ -structure.

#### Proposition 2.5 ( $\mu$ -ordinary Newton polygon for $K3$ surface).

Let $X/L$ be a K3 surface satisfying the assumptions (A1) and (A2). Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime in $S$ and $p=\mathfrak{p}\cap\mathbb{Z}$ . Let $d$ be as defined in Notation 2.3.

Then, $\mu_{\mathfrak{p}}$ has slopes $1-\frac{1}{d},1,1+\frac{1}{d}$ with multiplicities $d,22-2d,d$ .

Notice that if $d=1$ , equivalently if $p$ splits completely in $F$ , then the $\mu$ -ordinary Newton polygon coincides with the ordinary Newton polygon.

#### Proof.

Recall that $V=\mathrm{T}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ and $F$ acts on $V$ . Moreover, $\text{Fr}_{p}$ has order $d$ in $\mathrm{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ . Hence, $\mathrm{Hom}(F,\mathbb{C})$ splits into $[F:\mathbb{Q}]/d$ orbits, each of cardinality $d$ . Denote $\text{Fr}_{p}$ by $\sigma_{p}$ and $\tau\circ\sigma_{p}^{-1}$ by $\sigma_{p}\circ\tau$ , the Frobenius orbit of $\tau\in\mathrm{Hom}(F,\mathbb{C})$ is $\mathfrak{o}_{\tau}=\{\tau,\sigma_{p}\circ\tau,\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{d-1}\circ\tau\}$ .

We can decompose $V_{\mathbb{C}}$ into $\tau$ -eigenspaces:

$$ V_{\mathbb{C}}=\bigoplus_{\tau\in\mathrm{Hom}(F,\mathbb{C})}V_{\tau} $$

where $\dim_{\mathbb{C}}V_{\tau}=\begin{cases}n,&\text{if $F$ is CM},\\ 2n,&\text{if $F$ is totally real}.\end{cases}$ On the other hand, we have the Hodge decomposition

$$ V_{\mathbb{C}}=V^{2,0}\oplus V^{1,1}\oplus V^{0,2} $$

By the analogue of [7, Proposition 4.3] for weight 2 Hodge structure, the slopes of the $\mu$ -ordinary Newton polygons can be computed as follows. Write the Hodge slopes of $V_{\tau}$ in increasing order as $a_{\tau,1}\leq a_{\tau,2}\leq\cdots\leq a_{\tau,\dim(V_{\tau})}$ , then the $j$ -th $\mu$ -ordinary Newton slope associated with $\mathfrak{o}$ is

$$ \lambda_{\mathfrak{o},j}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}a_{\sigma_{p}^{i}\circ\tau,j},\qquad 1\leq j\leq\dim(V_{\tau}). $$

And each slope $\lambda_{\mathfrak{o},j}$ occurs with multiplicity $d$ .

We apply this formula to our setting. Let $\tau_{0}$ be the unique embedding such that $V_{\tau_{0}}\cap V^{0,2}\neq 0$ .

- (1) If $F$ is CM, then $\tau_{0}^{*}\neq\tau_{0}$ . The Hodge slopes of these two eigenspaces are

$$ V_{\tau_{0}}:\{0,1,\ldots,1\},\qquad V_{\tau_{0}^{*}}:\{1,\ldots,1,2\}, $$

while every other $V_{\tau}$ has Hodge slopes $\{1,\ldots,1\}$ . • If $\tau_{0}^{*}\not\in\mathfrak{o}_{\tau_{0}}$ . Then, the orbit $\mathfrak{o}_{\tau_{0}}$ contains one Hodge-slope list $\{0,1,\ldots,1\}$ and $d-1$ lists $\{1,\ldots,1\}$ . Hence

$$ \lambda_{\mathfrak{o}_{\tau_{0}},1}=\frac{0+(d-1)}{d}=1-\frac{1}{d}, $$

and all the other slopes associated with $\mathfrak{o}_{\tau_{0}}$ are equal to $1$ . Similarly, the orbit $\mathfrak{o}_{\tau_{0}^{*}}$ contains one list $\{1,\ldots,1,2\}$ and $d-1$ lists $\{1,\ldots,1\}$ , so

$$ \lambda_{\mathfrak{o}_{\tau_{0}^{*}},n}=\frac{2+(d-1)}{d}=1+\frac{1}{d}, $$

and all its other slopes are equal to $1$ . • If $\tau_{0}^{*}\in\mathfrak{o}_{\tau_{0}}$ . Then, this orbit contains the two lists $\{0,1,\ldots,1\},\{1,\ldots,1,2\}$ and $d-2$ lists $\{1,\ldots,1\}$ . By the above computation, $\lambda_{\mathfrak{o}_{\tau_{0}},1}=1-\frac{1}{d}$ , $\lambda_{\mathfrak{o}_{\tau_{0}},n}=1+\frac{1}{d}$ , and all the other slopes are $1$ . Thus, in either case, the exceptional Newton slopes are $1-\frac{1}{d}$ and $1+\frac{1}{d}$ each with multiplicity $d$ , while all remaining slopes are equal to $1$ .

- (2) Otherwise, we have $\tau_{0}^{*}=\tau_{0}$ , and the Hodge slopes of $V_{\tau_{0}}$ are $\{0,1,\ldots,1,2\}$ , while every other eigenspace again has slopes $\{1,\ldots,1\}$ . By Assumption $(A2)$ , we have $n\geq 2$ , so the positions containing $0$ and $2$ are distinct, so we have the same conclusion for the Newton slopes as in case 1.

In summary, we see that the Newton polygon of $T(X)$ has slopes $1-\frac{1}{d},1,1+\frac{1}{d}$ with multiplicities $d,2mn-2d,d$ . The $\text{NS}(X)$ part contributes $22-2mn$ additional copies of slope $1$ . Therefore, the full $\mu$ -ordinary Newton polygon has slopes $1-\frac{1}{d},1,1+\frac{1}{d}$ with multiplicities $d,22-2d,d$ , as desired. ∎

#### Definition 2.6.

Let $\mathfrak{p}\in S$ . We say $\mathfrak{p}$ is a $\mu$ -ordinary (resp. non- $\mu$ -ordinary) prime if the Newton polygon of the reduction $X_{\mathfrak{p}}$ coincides with $\mu_{\mathfrak{p}}$ (resp. does not coincide with $\mu_{\mathfrak{p}}$ ).

### 2.3. $l$ -adic monodromy group and connected field

We adapt the setup from [3, Section 2.3] to fit the framework of our paper.

Let $X/L$ be a K3 surface. We fix an embedding of $L$ into $\mathbb{C}$ and write $X_{\mathbb{C}}$ for the corresponding complex K3 surface. Let $X_{\overline{L}}$ denote the base change of $X$ to $\overline{L}$ . Fix a prime $l$ and consider the $l$ -adic representation on the étale cohomology:

$$ \rho_{X,l}:\text{Gal}(\overline{L}/L)\to\mathrm{GL}(H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})). $$

The $l$ -adic monodromy group, denoted by $G_{X,l}$ , is defined as the Zariski closure of the image of $\rho_{X,l}$ in $\mathrm{GL}(H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l}))$ . Let $G_{X,l}^{\circ}$ be the identity component of $G_{X,l}$ viewed as an algebraic group over $\mathbb{Q}_{l}$ . Let $\pi_{0}(G_{X,l})=G_{X,l}/G_{X,l}^{\circ}$ be the group of connected components of $G_{X,l}$ , which is a finite group.

#### Definition 2.7.

[3, Definition 2.4] $L^{\text{conn}}$ is the field extension of $L$ such that $\rho^{-1}_{X,l}(G^{\circ}_{X,l})=\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{L}/L^{\text{conn}}).$

By construction, $L^{\text{conn}}/L$ is finite Galois with $\mathrm{Gal}(L^{\text{conn}}/L)\simeq\pi_{0}(G_{X,l})$ . In particular, $L^{\text{conn}}$ is independent of the choice of $l$ .

We assume one further condition on $X/L$ in terms of $L^{\text{conn}}$ .

#### Assumption 2 (A3).

$L^{\text{conn}}\subseteq FL$ .

Under Assumptions $(A1)$ and $(A3)$ , since $\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)\xhookrightarrow{}\mathrm{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ and $\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)\twoheadrightarrow\mathrm{Gal}(L^{\text{conn}}/L)$ , we know that $\pi_{0}(G_{X,l})$ is a quotient of $\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ which is abelian. Moreover, each connected component in $\pi_{0}(G_{X,l})$ can be represented by some $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ .

### 2.4. Mumford-Tate conjecture on K3 surface

Let $\mathrm{MT}_{X}$ be the Mumford–Tate group of $X$ . Recall that $\mathrm{MT}(V,\Psi)$ is the smallest algebraic subgroup of $\mathrm{GO}(V,\Psi)$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ whose real points contain the image of the Hodge structure morphism $h:\mathbb{S}\longrightarrow\mathrm{GO}(V,\Psi)_{\mathbb{R}}$ .

Recall that we have the decomposition $\mathrm{H}^{2}(X,\mathbb{Q})=\text{NS}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\oplus\mathrm{T}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ and we let $V=\mathrm{T}(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}$ . The action of $\mathrm{MT}_{X}$ preserves both summands. On the Néron–Severi part, it acts through the weight character, which is already determined by its action on $V$ . Hence restriction to $V$ identifies $\mathrm{MT}_{X}$ with $\mathrm{MT}(V,\Psi)$ .

From the definition of $\mathrm{End}_{\text{Hdg}}(T(X)_{\mathbb{Q}})=\mathcal{E}(X)=F$ , we can further deduce that $\mathrm{MT}(V,\Psi)\subseteq\mathrm{GO}_{F}(V,\Psi)$ . Since $\mathrm{MT}(V,\Psi)$ is connected, we know that in fact it is contained in the identity component $\mathrm{GO}_{F}(V,\Psi)^{\circ}$ .

We have the following result of Zarhin stating that this containment is actually an isomorphism.

#### Theorem 2.8 (Zarhin, [18]).

Let $(V,\Psi)$ be an irreducible polarized rational Hodge structure of K3 type, and let $F=\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{Hdg}}(V)$ . Then,

$$ \mathrm{MT}(V,\Psi)=\mathrm{GO}_{F}(V,\Psi)^{\circ}. $$

On the other hand, the Mumford-Tate conjecture holds for K3 surface by the following result of Tankeev.

#### Theorem 2.9 (Tankeev,[16, 17]).

There exists a canonical isomorphism

$$ G_{X,l}^{\circ}\simeq\mathrm{MT}_{X}\otimes\mathbb{Q}_{l}. $$

Let $V_{l}:=V\otimes\mathbb{Q}_{l}\subset H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ together with the bilinear form $\Psi_{l}:=\Psi\otimes\mathbb{Q}_{l}$ . The Galois action preserves the Néron–Severi part and hence also preserves its orthogonal complement $V_{l}$ . Moreover, the Galois action on the Tate twist $\text{NS}(X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}_{l}(1)$ has finite image. Therefore, on the identity component $G_{X,l}^{\circ}$ , the action on the untwisted Néron–Severi part is through the cyclotomic character and is determined by the action on $V_{l}$ . Hence restriction to $V_{l}$ identifies $G_{X,l}^{\circ}$ with its image in $\mathrm{GO}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})$ . Combining the Mumford–Tate conjecture with Zarhin’s theorem, we obtain the following.

#### Corollary 2.10.

$G_{X,l}^{\circ}\cong\mathrm{GO}_{F}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})^{\circ}$

## 3. The $\mu$ -ordinary invariant $a_{\mathfrak{p}}$

In this section, we adapt the strategy of [3, Section 3] to the second cohomology of a K3 surface. The main idea is to construct a normalized Frobenius trace $a_{\mathfrak{p}}$ which detects whether a prime is $\mu$ -ordinary. The normalization removes the weight-two contribution from Frobenius, so that at a non- $\mu$ -ordinary prime $\mathfrak{p}$ , the resulting trace belongs to a finite set independent of $p$ .

Let $\chi$ denote the one-dimensional character of $G_{X,l}$ induced by the Galois action on the Tate twist $\mathbb{Q}_{l}(-1)$ . With our convention for Frobenius, for every degree-one prime $\mathfrak{p}$ above $p$ , we have $\chi(\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}})=p$ . For each prime $\mathfrak{p}\in S$ above a rational prime $p$ , the Frobenius $\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}\in\text{Gal}(\overline{L}/L)$ is well-defined up to conjugacy. By abuse of notation, let us also use $\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ for its image under $\rho_{X,l}$ .

Recall that $d=[F:K]$ , where $K$ is the largest subfield of $F$ over which $p$ splits completely. The trace on the algebraic representation $\wedge^{d}H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})\otimes\chi^{-d}$ gives a well-defined invariant:

$$ a_{\mathfrak{p}}:=\Tr(\Fr_{\mathfrak{p}} \mid\wedge^d H^2(X_{\overline{L}},\Q_l) \otimes\chi^{-d}). $$

#### Proposition 3.1.

If $\mathfrak{p}$ is not $\mu$ -ordinary, then $a_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is an integer in $[-\binom{22}{d},\binom{22}{d}]$ .

#### Proof.

The characteristic polynomial of $\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ acting on $H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ has the form

$$ P(T):=T^{22}+c_{1}T^{21}+\dots+c_{21}T+c_{22}. $$

By Deligne’s proof of the Weil conjectures [4, 5], the action of $\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is semisimple, and the coefficients $c_{i}$ are integers independent of $l$ . Let us split $P(T)$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ into

$$ P(T)=(T-\alpha_{1})\dots(T-\alpha_{22}). $$

From Weil’s conjecture, the $\alpha_{i}$ are algebraic integers with Archimedean absolute value $p$ and $\mathfrak{q}$ -adic units for any prime $\mathfrak{q}$ of $L$ away from $p$ .

By [1, Chapter 8], the $p$ -adic valuations of $\alpha_{i}$ are exactly the slopes of the Newton polygon $\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(X)$ . The trace of $\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ on $\wedge^{d}H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ is given by

$$ b:=\text{Tr}(\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}\mid\wedge^{d}H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l}))=\sum\limits_{I\subset\{1,\dots,22\},\#I=d}\prod_{i\in I}\alpha_{i} $$

Moreover, $b$ is an integer as it can be written as a polynomial with integer coefficients in the variables $c_{i}$ . Since $\mathfrak{p}$ is not $\mu$ -ordinary, by Proposition 2.5, the smallest slope of $\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(X)$ is greater than $1-\frac{1}{d}$ . Thus, the sum of any $d$ slopes of $\nu_{\mathfrak{p}}(X)$ is greater than $d-1$ , i.e., the $p$ -valuation of $\prod_{i\in I}\alpha_{i}$ is greater than $d-1$ . Hence, the $p$ -valuation of $b$ must be at least $d$ , or equivalently $p^{d}\mid b$ . In addition, as each $\alpha_{i}$ has absolute value $p$ , we deduce that

$$ -p^{d}\binom{22}{d}\leq b\leq p^{d}\binom{22}{d}. $$

Since $\chi(\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}})=p$ , we have that $a_{\mathfrak{p}}=\frac{b}{p^{d}}$ . Hence $a_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is an integer in $[-\binom{22}{d},\binom{22}{d}]$ ∎

We now relate the density of non- $\mu$ -ordinary primes to the behavior of certain algebraic trace functions on the connected components of $G_{X,l}$ . We will be using the following commutative diagram:

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{X,l}^{\circ}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\text{Gal}(\overline{L}/L)\ni\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{X,l}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\text{Gal}(FL/L)\ni\sigma} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\text{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{0}(G_{X,l})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\text{Gal}(L^{\text{conn}}/L).} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{X,l}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{0}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\kappa} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{X,l}} $$

Here $\kappa$ is induced by the inclusion $L^{\text{conn}}\subseteq FL$ , and $\iota$ is restriction to $F$ . By Assumption (A3), the map $\kappa$ is surjective, while $\iota$ is injective.

Let $S$ be the set of primes in $L$ in Definition 2.2. Let $S[\nu]:=\{\mathfrak{p}\in S:\mathfrak{p}\text{ is not $\mu$-ordinary}\}$ . For $A,B$ sets of primes in $L$ , let $\rho(A:B)$ be the density of $A$ in $B$ and $\rho(A)$ be the density of $A$ as in Definition 2.4.

We want to compute $\rho(S[\nu])$ . Equivalently, since $\rho(S)=1$ , we want to compute $\rho(S[\nu]:S)$ . For this purpose, we consider the following partition of $S$ :

$$ S=\coprod_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)}S_{\sigma}. $$

where $S_{\sigma}:=\left\{\mathfrak{p}\in S:\left.\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}\right|_{FL}=\sigma\right\}.$ Since $\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ is abelian, this condition is independent of the choice of the Frobenius element $\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ .

By the Chebotarev density theorem, we have that $\rho(S_{\sigma}:S)=\frac{1}{[FL:L]}$ for every $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ . Hence, it suffices to compute $\rho(S_{\sigma}[\nu]:S_{\sigma})$ , where $S_{\sigma}[\nu]=S_{\sigma}\cap S[\nu]$ .

Set $\Gamma:=\rho_{X,l}\bigl(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{L}/FL)\bigr)$ . Fix $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ , let $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ be the connected component of $G_{X,l}$ corresponding to $\sigma$ . For the same $\sigma$ , choose a lift $\widetilde{\sigma}\in\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{L}/L)$ and define $\Gamma_{\sigma}:=\rho_{X,l}(\widetilde{\sigma})\Gamma$ . Because $L^{\text{conn}}\subseteq FL$ , the subgroup $\Gamma$ is Zariski dense in $G_{X,l}^{\circ}$ . Hence, in this notation, we have:

$$ \overline{\Gamma}=G_{X,l}^{\circ}\qquad{}\overline{\Gamma}_{\sigma}=G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)} $$

#### Lemma 3.2 (Chebotarev–Serre).

Let $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ , let $\Gamma_{\sigma}$ be as defined above and let $\mu_{\sigma}$ be the translated Haar measure on $\Gamma_{\sigma}$ . Let $A\subseteq\Gamma_{\sigma}$ be a conjugacy invariant Borel subset whose boundary has $\mu_{\sigma}$ -measure zero. Then

$$ \rho\left(\left\{\mathfrak{p}\in S_{\sigma}:\rho_{X,l}(\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}})\in A\right\}:S_{\sigma}\right)=\mu_{\sigma}(A). $$

#### Proof.

This is the Chebotarev density theorem in the $l$ -adic setting; see [15, Corollary 6.10]. ∎

For $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ , for every $\mathfrak{p}\in S_{\sigma}$ , we have $\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}\mid_{F}=\iota(\sigma)$ . Hence $d=\operatorname{ord}\bigl(\iota(\sigma)\bigr)$ , which is constant as $\mathfrak{p}$ varies in $S_{\sigma}$ . Hence, we can define the conjugacy invariant algebraic function $b_{\sigma}$ on $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ as follows:

$$ b_{\sigma}:=\Tr( - \mid\wedge^d H^2(X_{\overline{L}},\Q_l) \otimes\chi^{-d}):G^{(\sigma)}_{X,l}\to\mathbb{Q}_{l}. $$

In particular, for every $\mathfrak{p}\in S_{\sigma}$ , one has $b_{\sigma}\bigl(\rho_{X,l}(\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}})\bigr)=a_{\mathfrak{p}}.$

#### Proposition 3.3.

The density of the set of non- $\mu$ -ordinary primes satisfies

$$ \rho(S[\nu]:S)\leq\frac{\#\left\{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L):b_{\sigma}\text{ is constant on }G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}\right\}}{[FL:L]}. $$

In particular, if $b_{\sigma}$ is nonconstant on $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ for every $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ , then the set of non- $\mu$ -ordinary primes has density zero.

#### Proof.

We have that $\rho(S[\nu]:S)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)}\rho(S_{\sigma}[\nu]:S_{\sigma})\rho(S_{\sigma}:S)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)}\frac{\rho(S_{\sigma}[\nu]:S_{\sigma})}{[FL:L]}$ . Hence, we need to show that

$$ \rho\bigl(S_{\sigma}[\nu]:S_{\sigma}\bigr)\leq\begin{cases}1,&\text{ if $b_{\sigma}$ is constant on }G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)},\\[2.84526pt]
0,&\text{ if $b_{\sigma}$ is nonconstant on }G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}.\end{cases} $$

Fix $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ and set $C=\binom{22}{d}$ . Consider the conjugacy-invariant closed subset

$$ Z^{\prime}_{\sigma}:=\bigcup_{n\in[-C,C]\cap\mathbb{Z}}b_{\sigma}^{-1}(n)\subseteq G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}. $$

And let $Z_{\sigma}=Z_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap\Gamma_{\sigma}$ . By Proposition 3.1, for every $\mathfrak{p}\in S_{\sigma}[\nu]$ , we have $\rho_{X,l}(\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}})\in Z_{\sigma}$ . Since $Z_{\sigma}$ is $l$ -adic analytic, we know that the boundary of $Z_{\sigma}$ has $\mu_{\sigma}$ measure zero. Hence, by Lemma 3.2 we have $\rho\bigl(S_{\sigma}[\nu]:S_{\sigma}\bigr)\leq\mu_{\sigma}\bigl(Z_{\sigma}\bigr)$ . Since $\Gamma_{\sigma}$ is Zariski dense in $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ , we have that $\mu_{\sigma}(Z_{\sigma})=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}\subseteq Z^{\prime}_{\sigma}$; }\\ 0&\text{ otherwise.}\\ \end{cases}$

Now we want to show that $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}\subseteq Z^{\prime}_{\sigma}$ if and only if $b_{\sigma}$ is constant on $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ .

Suppose $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}\subseteq Z^{\prime}_{\sigma}$ . Since $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ is connected, there exists $n\in[-C,C]$ such that $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}\subseteq b_{\sigma}^{-1}(n)$ . Hence, $b_{\sigma}$ is constant.

Conversely, if $b_{\sigma}$ is constant on $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ , with constant value $c$ . It suffices to show that $c\in[-C,C]\cap\mathbb{Z}$ . Write $c=\frac{x}{y}$ such that $\gcd(x,y)=1.$ By definition of $b_{\sigma}$ , we have that $c=\frac{b}{p^{d}}$ where recall that $b=\text{Tr}(\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}\mid\wedge^{d}H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l}))$ . Hence, $y\mid p^{d}$ , and this holds for every $\mathfrak{p}\in S_{\sigma}$ and $p=\mathfrak{p}\cap\mathbb{Z}$ . Therefore, since $S_{\sigma}$ has positive density, we can find $\mathfrak{p},\mathfrak{p}^{\prime}\in S_{\sigma}$ such that $p\neq p^{\prime}$ . Hence $y\mid p^{d}$ and $y\mid p^{\prime d}$ for two distinct primes $p,p^{\prime}$ . This implies that $y=1$ , hence $c$ is an integer. Moreover, the Weil bound $|b|\leq p^{d}C$ gives $c\in[-C,C]\cap\mathbb{Z}$ . This finishes the proof. ∎

## 4. Computation on the orthogonal group

In this section, we fix a connected component $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ represented by $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ and show that the trace function $b_{\sigma}$ is non-constant. By Proposition 3.3, this will imply that the set of non- $\mu$ -ordinary primes has density zero in $L$ . To prove the nonconstancy of $b_{\sigma}$ , we realize $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ as an explicit coset of matrices and compute $b_{\sigma}$ on this coset.

Recall from Corollary 2.10 that $G_{X,l}^{\circ}\simeq\mathrm{GO}_{F}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})^{\circ}$ . Since extending the coefficient field does not affect whether $b_{\sigma}$ is constant, we work over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l}$ for the remainder of this section. Set

$$ G:=\text{O}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})\otimes\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l},\qquad G_{F}:=\ker\left(\alpha:\mathrm{GO}_{F}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})^{\circ}\to\mathbb{Q}_{l}^{\times}\right)\otimes\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l} $$

where $\alpha$ is the orthogonal similitude character. In particular, $G_{F}\subseteq G_{X,l}^{\circ}\otimes\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l}$ .

If $B_{\sigma}$ is a representative of the connected component $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ , then $B_{\sigma}G_{F}\subseteq G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ . Hence, it suffices to prove that $b_{\sigma}$ is nonconstant on $B_{\sigma}G_{F}$ . This is analogous to the restriction to the similitude-one subgroup in the proof of [3, Theorem 4.19].

Recall from Notation 2.1 that $m=[F_{0}:\mathbb{Q}]$ and $2mn=\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}(V)$ .

When $F$ is CM, then $[F:\mathbb{Q}]=2m$ . For each $\sigma_{i}\in\mathrm{Hom}(F_{0},\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ , let $\tau_{i},\tau_{i}^{*}\in\mathrm{Hom}(F,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ be the two extensions of $\sigma_{i}$ . The $F$ -action gives a decomposition

$$ V_{l}\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}\left(V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}\oplus V_{l}^{\tau_{i}^{*}}\right), $$

where each $V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}$ and $V_{l}^{\tau_{i}^{*}}$ has dimension $n$ . Since the pairing $\Psi_{l}$ is $F$ -linear, we see that $V_{l}^{\tau}$ pairs nontrivially only with $V_{l}^{\tau^{*}}$ . Hence, after choosing suitable bases, for each $1\leq i\leq m$ , we may write $\Psi_{l}\big|_{V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}\oplus V_{l}^{\tau_{i}^{*}}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&J_{i}\\ J_{i}&0\end{pmatrix},$ where $J_{i}$ is some invertible diagonal matrix.

When $F$ is totally real, then

$$ V_{l}\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l}=\bigoplus_{\tau\in\mathrm{Hom}(F,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})}V_{l}^{\tau}, $$

where each $V_{l}^{\tau}$ has dimension $2n$ . In this case, the character spaces are mutually orthogonal with respect to $\Psi_{l}$ , and the restriction $\Psi_{l}\big|_{V_{l}^{\tau}}$ is a nondegenerate symmetric form on $V_{l}^{\tau}$ .

The preceding decompositions give the following block matrix description of $G_{F}$ .

#### Lemma 4.1.

After passing to $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l}$ , the following hold.

- (1) If $F$ is CM, then

$$ G_{F}\simeq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathrm{GL}_{n} $$

where the isomorphism is given by $\mathrm{diag}\left(M_{1},M_{1}^{*},\ldots,M_{m},M_{m}^{*}\right)\longmapsto(M_{1},\ldots,M_{m})$ with $M_{i}^{*}:=J_{i}^{-1}(M_{i}^{-1})^{\top}J_{i}$ .

- (2) If $F$ is totally real, then

$$ G_{F}\simeq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathrm{SO}_{2n} $$

where the isomorphism is given by $\mathrm{diag}(M_{1},\ldots,M_{m})\longmapsto(M_{1},\ldots,M_{m}),$ with $M_{i}^{\top}\Psi_{l}^{\tau_{i}}M_{i}=\Psi_{l}^{\tau_{i}}$ .

Next we consider the Weyl group of $G_{F}$ and $G$ . Let $T$ be the maximal torus of $G_{F}$ given by

$$ T=\left\{\mathrm{diag}(T_{1},T_{1}^{-1},\dots,T_{m},T_{m}^{-1})\,\middle|\,\text{$T_{i}$ is diagonal of size $n$}\right\}. $$

Since $T$ has rank $nm$ , it is also a maximal torus of $G$ .

We write $W_{F}$ for the Weyl group of $G_{F}$ with respect to $T$ , and $\widetilde{W}$ for the extended Weyl group of $G$ with respect to $T$ . That is,

$$ \widetilde{W}:=N_{G}(T)/T,\qquad W_{F}:=N_{G_{F}}(T)/T $$

We also set

$$ H:=(N_{G}(G_{F})\cap N_{G}(T))/T. $$

We have the following diagram for the inclusion relation among these various groups:

In particular, we have

$$ N_{G_{F}}(T)\subseteq N_{G}(T)\cap N_{G}(G_{F})\subseteq N_{G}(T) $$

Passing to the quotients by $T$ we get that $W_{F}\subseteq H\subseteq\widetilde{W}$ .

The extended Weyl group $\widetilde{W}$ can be realized as a subgroup of $\mathfrak{S}_{2mn}$ . More precisely, we identify

$$ \mathfrak{S}_{2mn}=\mathfrak{S}\{\pm 1,\pm 2,\dots,\pm mn\}, $$

where the subset $\{\pm(in-n+1),\dots,\pm in\}$ corresponds to the pair $(T_{i},T_{i}^{-1})$ . Then

$$ \widetilde{W}=\left\{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}\{\pm 1,\dots,\pm mn\}\,\middle|\,\pi(-i)=-\pi(i)\right\}. $$

And $W_{F}$ can be identified as a subgroup of $\widetilde{W}$ . By Lemma 4.1,

- • if $F$ is CM, then $\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cong W_{F}$ , with the isomorphism given by $(\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{m})\mapsto(\pi_{1},\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{m},\pi_{m})$ .

- • if $F$ is totally real, then $\prod_{i=1}^{m}W_{\mathrm{SO}_{2n}}\cong W_{F}$ .

The next proposition is an adaptation of [3, Proposition 4.14].

#### Proposition 4.2.

We have a natural isomorphism

$$ N_{G}(G_{F})/G_{F}\simeq H/W_{F}. $$

#### Proof.

We define a map from $N_{G}(G_{F})$ to $H/W_{F}$ whose kernel is $G_{F}$ . Let $g\in N_{G}(G_{F})$ , and consider $gTg^{-1}$ , which is a maximal torus of $G_{F}$ . Since maximal tori are conjugate, there exists $g_{0}\in G_{F}$ such that $gTg^{-1}=g_{0}Tg_{0}^{-1}$ , where $g_{0}$ is unique up to $N_{G_{F}}(T)$ . It follows that $g_{0}^{-1}g$ is in $N_{G}(G_{F})\cap N_{G}(T)$ , so the map

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}N_{G}(G_{F})&\to H/W_{F}\\
g&\mapsto g_{0}^{-1}gW_{F}\end{split} $$

is well-defined. It is surjective since $N_{G}(G_{F})\cap N_{G}(T)\subseteq N_{G}(G_{F})$ . The kernel of this map consists of $g$ such that $g_{0}^{-1}g\in N_{G_{F}}(T)$ , or $g\in G_{F}.$ ∎

The next lemma is an adaptation of [3, Lemma 4.15].

#### Lemma 4.3.

We have an isomorphism

$$ H/W_{F}\simeq\{\pm 1\}^{m}\rtimes\mathfrak{S}_{m}. $$

#### Proof.

- (1) If $F$ is CM, then by Lemma 4.1, $G_{F}\cong\prod_{m}\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ , where the $i$ -th copy of $\mathrm{GL}_{n}$ corresponds to the $i$ -th block $(M_{i},M_{i}^{*})$ in $G_{F}$ . Since $H$ normalizes $G_{F}$ , conjugation by $h\in H$ permutes the blocks of $G_{F}$ and possibly switches the pairs. Hence, $h\in H$ can be represented by $h=(\varepsilon_{1},\dots,\varepsilon_{m};\tau;\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{m})$ , where $\varepsilon_{i}\in\{\pm 1\},\pi_{i}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}$ . Since $W_{F}=\prod_{m}\mathfrak{S}_{n}$ , we get that $H/W_{F}=\{(\varepsilon_{1},\dots,\varepsilon_{m};\tau)\mid\varepsilon_{i}\in\{\pm 1\},\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}\}$ as desired.

- (2) If $F$ is totally real, then, by Lemma 4.1, $G_{F}\cong\prod_{m}\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$ . Since $H$ normalizes $G_{F}$ , $h\in H$ can be represented by $(\varepsilon_{1},\dots,\varepsilon_{m};\tau;w_{1},\dots,w_{m})$ where $\varepsilon_{i}\in\{\pm 1\},w_{i}\in W_{\mathrm{SO}_{2n}},\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}$ . Since $W_{F}=\prod_{m}W_{\mathrm{SO}_{2n}}$ , we get that $H/W_{F}$ is as desired.

∎

Fix a component $G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ and let $B_{\sigma}\in G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ be the representative. After multiplying $B_{\sigma}$ by a suitable scalar in $G_{X,l}^{\circ}$ , we may assume that $B_{\sigma}\in G$ . Since $G_{F}$ is the similitude-one subgroup of $G_{X,l}^{\circ}$ , it is normalized by $G_{X,l}$ , and hence $B_{\sigma}\in N_{G}(G_{F})$ and $B_{\sigma}G_{F}\subseteq G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ . By Proposition 4.2, we can find $B_{\sigma}^{\prime}\in N_{G}(T)\cap N_{G}(G_{F})$ such that $B_{\sigma}^{\prime}G_{F}=B_{\sigma}G_{F}$ . The class $B_{\sigma}^{\prime}T\in H$ determines an element $B_{\sigma}^{\prime}TW_{F}\in H/W_{F}$ . Let $P_{\sigma}\in\{\pm 1\}^{m}\rtimes\mathfrak{S}_{m}$ be the image of $B_{\sigma}^{\prime}TW_{F}$ under the isomorphism in Lemma 4.3. Thus $B_{\sigma}^{\prime}T\,W_{F}=P_{\sigma}T\,W_{F}$ . Hence, for some $n_{\sigma}\in N_{G_{F}}(T)$ , we have $n_{\sigma}^{-1}B_{\sigma}^{\prime}T=P_{\sigma}T$ . Therefore, for some $T_{\sigma}\in T$ , we have $n_{\sigma}^{-1}B_{\sigma}^{\prime}=P_{\sigma}T_{\sigma}$ . Since $n_{\sigma}\in G_{F}$ and $B_{\sigma}^{\prime}$ normalizes $G_{F}$ , we have $B_{\sigma}^{\prime}G_{F}=B_{\sigma}^{\prime}(B_{\sigma}^{\prime-1}n_{\sigma}^{-1}B_{\sigma}^{\prime})G_{F}=n_{\sigma}^{-1}B_{\sigma}^{\prime}G_{F}=P_{\sigma}T_{\sigma}G_{F}$ .

Thus we may choose $B_{\sigma}=P_{\sigma}T_{\sigma}$ where $P_{\sigma}\in\{\pm 1\}^{m}\rtimes\mathfrak{S}_{m}$ and $T_{\sigma}\in T$ , such that $B_{\sigma}G_{F}\subseteq G_{X,l}^{(\sigma)}$ .

For later use, we describe more explicitly the permutation represented by $P_{\sigma}$ . Recall that we have the following commutative diagram:

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)\ni\sigma} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{0}(G_{X,l})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{Gal}(L^{\text{conn}}/L).} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\kappa} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\iota} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho_{X,l}} $$

For any $\sigma\in\text{Gal}(FL/L)$ , its image in $\pi_{0}(G_{X,l})$ is $\rho_{X,l}(\kappa(\sigma))$ , while its image in $\text{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ is $\iota(\sigma)$ . Recall that $K=F^{\langle\iota(\sigma)\rangle}$ , so $d=[F:K]$ is equal to the order of $\iota(\sigma)$ in $\text{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ .

Notice that $\sigma$ acts on $\mathrm{Hom}(F,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ . For $\tau_{i}\in\mathrm{Hom}(F,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ , we denote the action of $\sigma$ via

$$ \sigma\cdot\tau_{i}=\tau_{i}\circ\iota(\sigma)^{-1} $$

This induces the action of the component $B_{\sigma}$ on the set of $F$ -eigenspaces by $B_{\sigma}(V_{l}^{\tau_{i}})=V_{l}^{\sigma\cdot\tau_{i}}$ . Since $F/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois and $\iota(\sigma)$ has order $d$ , every orbit of this action has length $d$ . Hence, when viewed as a permutation in $\mathfrak{S}_{2mn}$ , $P_{\sigma}$ has cycle type $(\underbrace{d,\dots,d}_{2mn/d}).$

We now describe how to obtain an element of $(\varepsilon_{1},\dots,\varepsilon_{m};\pi)\in\{\pm 1\}^{m}\rtimes\mathfrak{S}_{m}$ from $\sigma$ .

- • When $F$ is CM, write $\sigma_{i}=\tau_{i}|_{F_{0}}$ . Set $\sigma_{0}:=\iota(\sigma)|_{F_{0}}$ and $e:=\text{ord}(\sigma_{0})$ . The induced permutation $\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}$ is determined by $\sigma_{\pi(i)}=\sigma_{i}\circ\sigma_{0}^{-1}$ . Since $F_{0}/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois, every cycle of $\pi$ has length $e$ , so the cycle type of $\pi$ is $(\underbrace{e,\ldots,e}_{m/e\text{ times}})$ . We now define $\varepsilon_{i}$ . For each $i$ , either $\sigma\cdot\tau_{i}=\tau_{\pi(i)}$ or $\tau_{\pi(i)}^{*}$ . We define

$$ \varepsilon_{i}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{ if }\sigma\cdot\tau_{i}=\tau_{\pi(i)},\\ -1,&\text{ if }\sigma\cdot\tau_{i}=\tau_{\pi(i)}^{*}.\end{cases} $$

Thus $P_{\sigma}$ corresponds to the signed permutation $(\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{m};\pi)\in\{\pm 1\}^{m}\rtimes\mathfrak{S}_{m}$ . Notice that $e=d$ or $\frac{d}{2}$ . If $e=d$ , then the $\sigma$ -orbit of $\tau_{i}$ and $\tau_{i}^{*}$ are disjoint and each has length $d$ ; if $e=\frac{d}{2}$ , then we have $\iota(\sigma)^{e}=c$ where $c$ is the complex conjugation, so the $\sigma$ -orbit of $\tau_{i}$ is $\{\sigma^{j}\cdot\tau_{i}:0\leq j<e\}\sqcup\{\sigma^{j}\cdot\tau_{i}^{*}:0\leq j<e\}$ , which is a union of two size $e$ subsets.

- • When $F$ is totally real, we have $F_{0}=F$ , so $e=d$ . The permutation $\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}$ is similarly determined by $\tau_{\pi(i)}=\sigma\cdot\tau_{i}$ for $\tau_{i}\in\mathrm{Hom}(F,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ and has cycle type $(\underbrace{d,\ldots,d}_{m/d\text{ times}})$ . For each $i$ , the restriction of $P_{\sigma}$ gives an orthogonal isomorphism $P_{\sigma}|_{V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}}:V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}\longrightarrow V_{l}^{\tau_{\pi(i)}}$ . With respect to the chosen compatible orthogonal bases, we define

$$ \varepsilon_{i}:=\det\left(P_{\sigma}|_{V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}}\right)\in\{\pm 1\}. $$

Thus $P_{\sigma}$ corresponds to the signed permutation $(\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{m};\pi)\in\{\pm 1\}^{m}\rtimes\mathfrak{S}_{m}$ . The $\sigma$ -orbit of $\tau_{i}$ has length $d$ , just as in the case where $F$ is CM and $e=d$ .

#### Proposition 4.4.

For any $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(FL/L)$ , the function

$$ b_{\sigma}=\Tr\left(-\,\middle|\,\wedge^{d}H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})\otimes\chi^{-d}\right):B_{\sigma}G_{F}\longrightarrow\mathbb{Q}_{l} $$

is non-constant.

#### Proof.

Since $T_{\sigma}\in T\subset G_{F}$ , replacing $A$ by $T_{\sigma}A$ allows us to absorb $T_{\sigma}$ . It therefore suffices to find a one-parameter family $A(t)\in G_{F}$ such that, for $M(t):=P_{\sigma}A(t)$ , the function

$$ b_{\sigma}(M(t))=\Tr\left(M(t)\,\middle|\,\wedge^{d}H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})\right) $$

is nonconstant in $t$ . Since we are working on the similitude-one subgroup, we suppress the factor $\chi^{-d}$ .

- (1) Suppose $F$ is CM. By Lemma 4.1,

$$ A=\mathrm{diag}(A_{1},A_{1}^{*},\ldots,A_{m},A_{m}^{*}),\qquad A_{i}^{*}=J_{i}^{-1}(A_{i}^{-1})^{\top}J_{i}. $$

where each $A_{i}$ is of size $n\times n$ . We take $A(t)=\mathrm{diag}(A_{1}(t),A_{1}(t)^{*},\text{I}_{n},\text{I}_{n},\ldots,\text{I}_{n},\text{I}_{n})$ . Let

$$ p_{k}(t):=\Tr\left(M(t)^{k}\,\middle|\,V_{l}\right),\qquad E_{j}(t):=\Tr\left(M(t)\,\middle|\,\wedge^{j}V_{l}\right) $$

Since $M(t)^{k}:V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}\to V_{l}^{\sigma^{k}\cdot\tau_{i}}$ and the $\sigma$ -orbit of $\tau_{i}$ has length $d$ , we have that $p_{k}(t)=0$ for $1\leq k<d$ . By Newton’s identities, we have $jE_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{j}(-1)^{k-1}E_{j-k}p_{k}$ . Hence we have $E_{j}(t)=0$ for $1\leq j<d$ and $E_{d}(t)=\frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{d}\,p_{d}(t)$ . Now recall that $H^{2}(X_{\overline{L}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})=V_{l}\oplus\text{NS}_{l}$ , where $\text{NS}_{l}:=\text{NS}(X_{\overline{L}})\otimes\mathbb{Q}_{l}$ , and $M(t)$ on $\text{NS}_{l}$ is constant. Therefore,

$$ \begin{split}\Tr\left(M(t)\,\middle|\,\wedge^{d}H^{2}\right)&=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\Tr\left(M(t)\,\middle|\,\wedge^{j}V_{l}\right)\Tr\left(M(t)\,\middle|\,\wedge^{d-j}\text{NS}_{l}\right)\\ &=\Tr\left(M(t)\,\middle|\,\wedge^{d}V_{l}\right)+\Tr\left(M(t)\,\middle|\,\wedge^{d}\text{NS}_{l}\right)\\ &=k_{\sigma}+\frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{d}\,p_{d}(t)\end{split} $$

where $k_{\sigma}$ is the contribution from $\wedge^{d}\text{NS}_{l}$ and is independent of $t$ . Thus it remains to show that $p_{d}(t)=\Tr\left(M(t)^{d}\,\middle|\,V_{l}\right)$ is nonconstant. (a) Suppose first that $d=e$ . Then recall that the $\sigma$ -orbits of $\tau_{1}$ and $\tau_{1}^{*}$ are disjoint and each has length $d$ . Therefore,

$$ M(t)^{d}\mid_{V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}}=\begin{cases}A_{1}&\text{ if $\tau_{i}$ is in the $\sigma$-orbit of $\tau_{1}$}\\ A_{1}^{*}&\text{ if $\tau_{i}$ is in the $\sigma$-orbit of $\tau_{1}^{*}$}\\ I_{n}&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases} $$

Hence $p_{d}(t)=d\left(\Tr(A_1(t))+\Tr(A_1^*(t))\right)+(2m-2d)n$ . Take $A_{1}(t)=\mathrm{diag}(t,1,\ldots,1)$ . Since $J_{1}$ is diagonal, we have $A_{1}(t)^{*}=\mathrm{diag}(t^{-1},1,\ldots,1)$ . Therefore,

$$ p_{d}(t)=2mn+d(t+t^{-1}-2), $$

which is non-constant in $t$ . (b) Suppose $d=2e$ . Then $\tau_{i}$ and $\tau_{i}^{*}$ are in the same $\sigma$ -orbit of length $d$ . Therefore,

$$ M(t)^{d}\big|_{V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}}=\begin{cases}A_{1}A_{1}^{*}&\text{if $\tau_{i}=\sigma^{j}\cdot\tau_{1}$ for some $0\leq j<e$,}\\ A_{1}^{*}A_{1}&\text{if $\tau_{i}=\sigma^{j}\cdot\tau_{1}^{*}$ for some $0\leq j<e$,}\\ I_{n}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Hence $p_{d}(t)=d\Tr\left(A_{1}(t)A_{1}(t)^{*}\right)+(2m-d)n$ . Take $A_{1}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}\oplus I_{n-2}$ . Write $J_{1}=\mathrm{diag}(j_{1},j_{2},\dots,j_{n})$ , then $\Tr\left(A_{1}(t)A_{1}(t)^{*}\right)=n-\frac{j_{1}}{j_{2}}t^{2}$ , and hence

$$ p_{d}(t)=2mn-d\frac{j_{1}}{j_{2}}t^{2}, $$

which is nonconstant in $t$ .

- (2) Suppose $F$ is totally real. By Lemma 4.1,

$$ A=\mathrm{diag}(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}),\qquad A_{i}\in\mathrm{SO}_{2n}. $$

We take $A(t)=\mathrm{diag}(A_{1}(t),I_{2n},\ldots,I_{2n})$ . The action of $P_{\sigma}$ on the set of character spaces has cycles of length $d$ , so the same argument as above gives $\Tr\left(M(t)\,\middle|\,\wedge^{d}H^{2}\right)=k_{\sigma}+\frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{d}\,p_{d}(t)$ . By the same argument as the case where $d=e$ , we have $M(t)^{d}\mid_{V_{l}^{\tau_{i}}}=A_{1}$ when $\tau_{i}$ is in the $\sigma$ -orbit of $\tau_{1}$ and is $\text{I}_{2n}$ otherwise. Hence, $p_{d}(t)=d\Tr(A_1(t))+2n(m-d)$ . Take $A_{1}(t)=\mathrm{diag}(t)\oplus\text{I}_{n-1}\oplus\mathrm{diag}(t^{-1})\oplus\text{I}_{n-1}\in\mathrm{SO}_{2n}$ . Then

$$ p_{d}(t)=2mn+d(t+t^{-1}-2), $$

which is nonconstant in $t$ .

Therefore $b_{\sigma}$ is non-constant on $B_{\sigma}G_{F}$ . ∎

Propositions 3.3 and 4.4 imply the following theorem:

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $X$ be a K3 surface over a number field $L$ satisfying $(A1),(A2)$ and $(A3)$ . Then $\rho(S[\nu])=0$ . That is, the set of primes of $L$ with $\mu$ -ordinary reduction has density 1.

#### Corollary 1.2.

Let $X$ be a $K3$ surface over a number field $L$ satisfying $(A1),(A2)$ and $(A3)$ . Then, the set of primes of $L$ with ordinary reduction has density $\frac{1}{[FL:L]}$ .

#### Proof.

Because the $\mu$ -ordinary polygon is ordinary if and only if $p$ is totally split in $F/\mathbb{Q}$ , the set of ordinary primes of $L$ is the set of primes $\mathfrak{p}$ such that $\iota(\text{Fr}_{\mathfrak{p}}|_{FL})$ is the identity element in $\text{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ . This set has density $\frac{1}{[FL:L]}$ by Chebotarev’s density theorem.

∎

To show that the assumptions of Theorem 1.1 are non-vacuous, we exhibit an explicit one-dimensional family of K3 surfaces whose generic members satisfy assumptions $(A1),(A2)$ and $(A3)$ .

#### Example 4.5.

Consider the $1$ -dimensional family of curves $C_{\alpha}$ together with the fixed cover $D$ :

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}C_{\alpha}:y^{5}&=x(x-1)(x-\alpha),\qquad\alpha\neq 0,1\\
D:z^{5}&=t(t-1)\\
\end{split} $$

Both $C_{\alpha}$ and $D$ are $\mu_{5}$ -covers of $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and hence admit the natural $\mu_{5}$ -action. Notice that $C_{\alpha}$ is Moonen’s special family $M[11]$ in [9, Table 1].

Consider the $\mu_{5}$ -action on $C_{\alpha}\times D$ given by

$$ \zeta_{5}\cdot(x,y,t,z)=(x,\zeta_{5}y,t,\zeta_{5}^{-1}z). $$

Consider the GIT quotient $S_{\alpha}:=(C_{\alpha}\times D)/\mu_{5}$ , and let $X_{\alpha}$ be the minimal model of the resolution of $S_{\alpha}$ . The surface $S_{\alpha}$ has only cyclic quotient singularities. By the standard Hirzebruch–Jung resolution computation in [11, Section 1.2], one obtains $K_{X_{\alpha}}^{2}=0$ . Furthermore, by the signature formula in [7, Equation (2.4)] and the Künneth formula, one obtains $h^{2,0}(X_{\alpha})=1$ and $h^{1,0}(X_{\alpha})=0$ . By the classification of product-quotient K3 surfaces in [6, Theorem 5.1 and Table 1], we see that $X_{\alpha}$ is a K3 surface.

Fix a number field $L$ and choose $\alpha\in L$ such that $C_{\alpha}$ is generic. That is, $J(C_{\alpha})$ has no extra endomorphisms beyond those induced by the natural action of $\mu_{5}$ . We now verify that $X_{\alpha}$ satisfies assumptions $(A1)$ – $(A3)$ .

Since $C_{\alpha}$ is generic, we have $F:=\mathcal{E}(X_{\alpha})=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{5})$ , so $F/\mathbb{Q}$ is abelian and $(A1)$ holds. Since $F=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{5})$ is a CM field and the generic member $X_{\alpha}$ is non-CM, $(A2)$ holds.

It remains to verify $(A3)$ . For any $g\in\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{L}/FL)$ , the $F$ -action is defined over $FL$ , so $\rho_{X_{\alpha},l}(g)$ commutes with the image of $F$ . Hence $\rho_{X_{\alpha},l}(g)\in\operatorname{Cent}_{\mathrm{GO}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})}(F)=\mathrm{GO}_{F}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})$ .

Since $F$ is CM, by the discussion at the start of Section 4,

$$ \mathrm{GO}_{F}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l}\simeq\mathbb{G}_{m}\times\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathrm{GL}_{n}. $$

Thus $\mathrm{GO}_{F}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})$ is connected, and by Corollary 2.10, $\mathrm{GO}_{F}(V_{l},\Psi_{l})=G_{X_{\alpha},l}^{\circ}$ . Therefore,

$$ \rho_{X_{\alpha},l}\bigl(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{L}/FL)\bigr)\subseteq G_{X_{\alpha},l}^{\circ}, $$

so $L^{\text{conn}}\subseteq FL$ . Hence $(A3)$ holds.

For a generic K3 surface in the family, Theorem 1.1 implies that the density of primes of $L$ at which $X_{\alpha}$ has $\mu$ -ordinary reduction is $1$ . By Corollary 1.2, the density of ordinary primes is

$$ \frac{1}{[FL:L]}=\begin{cases}1,&L\supseteq\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{5}),\\
\frac{1}{2},&L\cap\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{5})=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5}),\\
\frac{1}{4},&L\cap\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{5})=\mathbb{Q}.\end{cases} $$
